# Energy prices {#sec-prices}

This chapter explains how the model builds the price of every fuel in every sector, year by year. Prices are the
first link of the model's chain: a carbon tax, an ETS, an excise reform or a subsidy reform changes fuel use, power
dispatch, emissions and revenue only through the prices computed here.

The chapter follows the order of the calculation. It starts with international prices, builds the domestic price
before new policies (supply cost, excise and other taxes, VAT), adds the existing carbon pricing, the subsidy and
price-control reforms and the new policies, and ends with the average prices and price indices that the model
reports. The welfare use of the Pigouvian prices and the revenue raised at these prices belong to
@sec-fiscal; electricity prices belong to @sec-power.

The methodology describes prices in
[methodology, section 3.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PricesAndTaxes) and, in more
detail, in [Appendix C](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-Appendix_C_Prices). This chapter
says where the model follows, simplifies or departs from it.

**Assumptions you need here.** The notation, dimensions and policy paths are set out in @sec-model-overview. Four
of them matter for every equation of this chapter:

- Every price, tax and policy value is in **real USD of the results year** $R$ (`ResultsYear`, 2026), per GJ unless
  stated. A constant real price is a constant number; fuel use responds only to real price changes.
- Prices up to the **last historical price year** $L$ (Settings `LastHistPriceYear`, default 2024, as legacy) are
  data; later years are projected. Fuel use is data in the base year $t_0 = 2022$ and modelled from 2023.
- Each equation holds for every scenario $o$ and country $c$; both indices are omitted. Scenario 1 is the baseline.
- Prices are quantity-free: everything up to the after-tax price is computed for all years before the year loop.
  Only the averages of @sec-pr-averages read fuel use, and they are computed inside the year loop.

## The price chain at a glance {#sec-pr-overview}

A fuel price is built in layers. The first layers are prices **before new policies**: what the country pays today,
projected forward with the international price. The last layers are **wedges** that policies add, each passed
through to the consumer with VAT.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    GP["International price gp"] --> SP["Supply cost sp"]
    PS["Producer subsidy ps"] --> SP
    SP --> TXO["Excise and other taxes txo<br/>(pass-through pcc)"]
    TXO --> PBC["Price before new policies pbc<br/>(sp + txo) x (1 + VAT)"]
    PBC --> ATP["After-tax price atp"]
    NCE["New policies nce<br/>carbon tax, ETS cost, excise"] --> ATP
    XCP["Change in existing<br/>carbon pricing xcpd"] --> ATP
    W["Subsidy and price-control<br/>wedges csw, pcw"] --> ATP
    ATP --> D["Fuel use (sec-demand)"]
    SHP["Shadow price shp"] --> D
```

| Step | Computes | Codes | By | Equations | Section |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | International price of each commodity | `gpn`, `gp` | commodity | A2.3 | @sec-pr-international |
| 2 | Historical domestic prices and forecasting coefficients | `sp`, `txo` ($t \le L$), `spf`, `pcc`, VAT rate | price block | A2.4 | @sec-pr-history |
| 3 | Producer subsidy per unit | `pros`, `psd`, `psu`, `ps` | fuel, price block | A2.5 | @sec-pr-producer |
| 4 | Supply cost | `sp` | price block | M2.1 | @sec-pr-supply |
| 5 | Excise and other taxes | `txf`, `txo` | price block | M2.2, A2.1 | @sec-pr-txo |
| 6 | VAT and the price before new policies; existing taxes and subsidies | `vat`, `pbc`, `etx`, `esub`, `esubpu`, `fadtx`, `cs` | price block | M2.3 | @sec-pr-pbc |
| 7 | Subsidy and price-control wedges | `pof`, `csf`, `pcf`, `pcsw`, `ppcw` | price block | M1.7 | @sec-pr-phaseouts |
| 8 | Existing carbon pricing | `xcp`, `xcpd` | subsector and fuel | A2.2 | @sec-pr-ecp |
| 9 | New policies, after-tax price, shadow price | `ctxnew`, `ets`, `ntx`, `nce`, `atp`, `shp` | subsector and fuel | M2.4-M2.6 | @sec-pr-atp, @sec-pr-shadow |
| 10 | Pigouvian components | `pig.*`, `cc.code`, `pigx`, `ntxb` | price block | A1.2 | @sec-pr-pigou |
| 11 | Averages and price indices (year loop) | `pnq` ... `rpn`, `pav.*`, `rpe` | price block, fuel | A2.6 | @sec-pr-averages |

The methodology writes the same identity in its own terms:
retail price = supply price + VAT + excise and other taxes, with the excise term holding every carbon price and
subsidy ([methodology, section 3.2.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PricesOVerview)). The
model keeps the same identity but stores the pieces separately: `txo` holds only the existing taxes and subsidies,
and the carbon prices and reforms are wedges on top (@sec-pr-atp).

## Price blocks: fuels and price sectors {#sec-pr-blocks}

Prices are kept by **price block**: a fuel and a price sector, as in the IMF price dataset. There are 12 blocks.
Coal and natural gas have one block each for power, residential and industry; the oil products and biomass have a
single block for all sectors. Electricity prices are left to the power module (@sec-power), but the electricity
rows `ecy.res` and `ecy.ind` appear where a policy path is set per price fuel (fuel price reform, Pigouvian taxes),
which makes 14 policy rows.

| Block | Fuel | Price unit | GJ per price unit $u$ | International commodity (`gp` position) | VAT where the data are blank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `coa.pow`, `coa.res`, `coa.ind` | Coal | USD/GJ | 1 | coal (2) | general rate for `coa.res`; 0 for power and industry |
| `nga.pow`, `nga.res`, `nga.ind` | Natural gas | USD/GJ | 1 | gas of the country's market (3) | general rate for `nga.res`; 0 for power and industry |
| `gso.all` | Gasoline | USD/liter | 0.03497 | crude oil (1) | general rate × household share |
| `die.all` | Diesel | USD/liter | 0.03730 | crude oil (1) | general rate × household share |
| `lpg.all` | LPG | USD/liter | 0.02578 | crude oil (1) | general rate × household share |
| `ker.all` | Kerosene (also jet fuel) | USD/liter | 0.03775 | crude oil (1) | general rate × household share |
| `oop.all` | Other oil products | USD/bbl | 6.12 | crude oil (1) | general rate |
| `bio.all` | Biomass | USD/GJ | 1 | flat 1 (4) | 0 |

: The 12 price blocks {#tbl-pr-blocks}

Each of the 16 subsectors takes the price of its **price sector**. Coal and gas use the block of that price sector;
every other fuel uses its `.all` block, whatever the subsector. Jet fuel is priced at the kerosene block (with its own
GJ per liter, 0.03486).

| Subsectors | Price sector for coal and gas |
|---|---|
| Road, residential | residential (`res`) |
| Rail, domestic aviation, domestic navigation | industry (`ind`) |
| Food and forestry, services | industry (`ind`) |
| Mining and chemicals, iron and steel, other metals, machinery, cement, other manufacturing, construction, fuel transformation, other energy use | industry (`ind`) |
| Power generation (power module) | power (`pow`) |

: Price sector of each subsector {#tbl-pr-subsectors}

The road and residential sectors therefore pay the residential coal and gas prices; food, services and the transport
modes other than road pay the industry prices.

**Layout of a block, as a model concept.** Each block is a small stack of rows that reads from top to bottom:

1. its settings: the pass-through, the VAT rate, GJ per price unit and the position of its international price;
2. the international reference price `gpi`, the fixed supply cost `spf`, the producer subsidy `ps`;
3. the build-up before new policies: `sp`, `txf`, `txo`, `fadtx`, `cs`, `etx`, `esub`, `esubpu`, `vat`, ending
   with `pbc`, the retail price before new policies;
4. the subsidy-reform wedges `pcsw` and `ppcw`;
5. the new policies averaged over the subsectors priced by the block (`pnq`, `pctx`, `etsnew`, `pntx`, `pxcd`,
   `pvatn`, `pnce`) and the retail price including new policies `rpn` (@sec-pr-averages).

New policies themselves act by subsector and fuel (rows 9 of the chain), because coverage, exemptions and emission
factors differ by subsector. The block shows their fuel-use weighted averages.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 2: one block of rows per price fuel | sector (Formulas E236-E281); the
  block parameters (`pset`, E242) come from sheet Inputs_prices (Inputs rows 158-169: pass-through K, VAT rate V,
  GJ per price unit G, international price position F). The subsector rows (sections 5-8) find their block by the
  price position in Inputs column U.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/prices_data.py` (`PRICES`, the 12 blocks), `core/excel_ai/fuels.csv`
  (units, GJ per unit, price fuel) and `subsectors.csv` (price sector, ECP sector); the fuel | subsector table is
  `fuel_data.fuel_table()`.
:::

## Units, real values and the two indices {#sec-pr-units}

All money values are converted to real USD of the results year as soon as they are read. Two different indices do the
conversion, both equal to 1 in the results year:

$$
\iota_t = \frac{\text{CPI}^{US}_R}{\text{CPI}^{US}_t}, \qquad \delta_t = \frac{\text{Defl}^{US}_R}{\text{Defl}^{US}_t}
$$ {#eq-pr-indices}

where

- $\iota_t$ is the **CPI index** (code `infl`; US CPI from the IMF WEO), used for nominal *domestic* values: the IMF
  price dataset, margins and production costs, producer subsidies, existing carbon tax rates and permit prices, and a
  nominal carbon price;
- $\delta_t$ is the **deflator index** (code `defl`; US GDP deflator, WEO), used for nominal *international* prices;
- $R$ is the results year (2026).

This is the legacy split (legacy rows 456/725 for the CPI index, 467 for the deflator). The two differ by up to 1.2%
before 2030 (2022: 1.137 against 1.124; 2030: 0.918 against 0.929), so one index alone would not reproduce legacy. The
CPI index is held flat after 2031 (the WEO horizon); the deflator is not.

**Where each input comes from, and in what units.**

| Input | Stored as | Converted with |
|---|---|---|
| Domestic prices (IMF dataset `Prices_dom`: supply cost, excise and other taxes, retail price) | nominal USD of their own year, per price unit | CPI index of that year, then ÷ GJ per price unit |
| Margins over international prices, domestic production costs | nominal USD of their data year | CPI index of their data year, then held constant in real terms |
| International prices (by source) | nominal, source units (USD/bbl, USD/t, USD/MMBtu) | deflator index; only their year-on-year ratio is used, so units drop out |
| Policy inputs on ScenarioDefinition (carbon price, feebates, fuel price reform) | real USD of the results year, in price units | none; only the carbon price has a nominal option (`NomorReal` = Nominal, then × CPI index; legacy row 2249) |
| Existing carbon tax rates and ETS prices (sheet ECP) | nominal USD of the data year | CPI index of the data year |
| Producer subsidies (`mit.pros.<fuel>.all`) | USD billion nominal | CPI index of the year, × 1000 (USD million) |

The model computes to 2041 (the legacy horizon of the power block). Values after 2030 are not compared with legacy:
the legacy CPI is flat after 2031 and some legacy rules misbehave over long horizons.

## International prices {#sec-pr-international}

International prices drive the projection of every supply cost. The model reads a forecast of each commodity from the
source chosen for the scenario, converts it to real terms and applies the High or Low adjustment. The methodology
describes the sources in
[Appendix C, choices of the sources](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#choices-of-the-sources-for-key-inputs).

$$
gp_{m,t} = gpn_{m,t}\;\delta_t\;h_{m,t}, \qquad
h_{m,t} = \begin{cases} 1 & t \le L \text{ or Base} \\ h^{High}_m \text{ or } h^{Low}_m & t > L \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pr-gp}

where

- $gp_{m,t}$ is the real international price of commodity $m$ (code `gp`, source units);
- $gpn_{m,t}$ is the nominal price of $m$ from the chosen source (code `gpn`; equation list
  [A2.3](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A2-3)); it is 1 for biomass, whose "commodity" is a flat line;
- $\delta_t$ is the deflator index (@eq-pr-indices);
- $h_{m,t}$ is the adjustment factor (code `gp.adj` holds the choice: 1 none, 2 High, 3 Low).

The commodity $m$ of a block is crude oil for the five oil products, coal for coal, the gas of the **country's gas
market** for natural gas, and the flat line for biomass. The block reads its commodity's price as its reference
price `gpi`.

| Commodity | High factor | Low factor |
|---|---|---|
| Crude oil | 1.5 | 0.5 |
| Coal | 1.25 | 0.75 |
| Natural gas (country's market) | 1.25 | 0.75 |
| Flat (biomass) | 1 | 1 |

: High / Low adjustments after the last historical year (sheet Constants `gp.hi`, `gp.lo`) {#tbl-pr-highlow}

**Choice of source.** ScenarioDefinition `IntEnerPricForeSource` names the source; the asterisk of a default
option is dropped (`IMF-WB*` is the average of IMF and WB). `IntEnerPricForecastAdjustment` chooses Base, High or
Low. Both are per scenario. The Egypt runs use IMF.

**The series by source.** Each series covers 2021-2045. Up to a source's last data year the series is data; after
it the series is extended by one of two rules.

| Source | Oil | Coal | Gas: LNG | Gas: North America | Gas: Europe | Extended from | Extension rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IMF | POILBRE | PCOALAU | PNGASJP | PNGASUS | PNGASEU | 2032 | × (1 + US GDP deflator inflation) |
| WB | Crude oil, Brent | Coal, Australia | LNG, Japan | Natural gas, US | Natural gas, Europe | 2027 | × (1 + US GDP deflator inflation) |
| IEA | Crude oil, avg | Coal, Australia | LNG, Japan | Natural gas, US | Natural gas, Europe | coal 2031; others beyond the horizon | × (1 + US GDP deflator inflation) |
| EIA | Brent | Coal (metric ton) | the IEA series | Henry hub | the IEA series | coal 2041; oil and gas beyond the horizon | × last growth factor $P_{t-1}/P_{t-2}$ |
| AVG | average of EIA, IEA, WB, IMF | same | IEA, WB, IMF | EIA, IEA, WB, IMF | IEA, WB, IMF | | |
| IMF-IEA, IMF-WB | average of the two | | | | | | |
| Manual | IMF before 2026, then sheet `Manual inputs` D221:AF225 (legacy addresses, by label and year) | | | | | | |

: International price series (Excel-AI sheet Inputs_pint; legacy Mitigation rows 633-695) {#tbl-pr-sources}

In words: the extension keeps a series constant in real terms (growth with US inflation), except EIA, which continues
its own last trend. Averages skip a missing source. A blank data cell reads as 0; a year past a series' data and before
its extension year reads as missing. The **global gas** price is the average of LNG, North America and Europe (under
Manual, the IMF global price before 2026).

**The country's gas market** comes from sheet Prices_int (regional assumptions, "Natural gas market assumption"):
*LNG* reads the LNG series, *Europe* the Europe series shifting to LNG (@sec-pr-lng), *North Am* the North American
series, and any other value the global average. Egypt's market is *Global*.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: international prices"}
```
src = IntEnerPricForeSource.replace('*', '')
adj = 'High' / 'Low' / none                       # IntEnerPricForecastAdjustment
for m in ['oil', 'coa', 'nga', 'one']:
    for t in years:
        if m == 'one':
            gp[m][t] = 1.0
            continue
        com = gas_market if m == 'nga' else m     # lng, eus, nam or glo
        gpn[m][t] = series[src][com][t]           # nominal, extended past the data
        factor = gp_hi[m] if adj == 'High' else gp_lo[m] if adj == 'Low' else 1
        gp[m][t] = gpn[m][t] * defl[t] * (factor if t > L else 1)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Inputs_pint (the series by source; `build_inputs_pint`), sheet Prices_int (regional
  assumptions, gas market; Settings C12 = `eus` for Europe markets); sheet Mitigation section 2 rows `gp.src`,
  `gp.adj`, `gpn`, `gp`, `gpi` (Formulas E238-E243). Inputs: ScenarioDefinition `IntEnerPricForeSource` (MTInputs
  row 220), `IntEnerPricForecastAdjustment` (row 258); sheet Constants `gp.hi|<m>`, `gp.lo|<m>`.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/prices_data.py`, `international_prices()` and `gas_market()`;
  `prices.py`, `prepare()` (first part); equation A2.3.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **M20 (prototype bug, fixed in Excel-AI 0.9.2).** The World Bank and IEA LNG and Europe gas series were read by
  position, so LNG and Europe were swapped. Each series is now read by its name; the IEA block is read by its World
  Bank labels because its own gas labels are swapped (the values under "Natural Gas - LNG" are the European price,
  IMF PNGASEU).
- **Past the IEA data (2041 on).** Excel-AI reads a misaligned cell there (equation list: issue I152); CPAT Python
  leaves the value missing. No effect within the model horizon.
:::

## Europe gas market: shift to LNG {#sec-pr-lng}

For countries in the European gas market the model follows Europe's move away from Russian pipeline gas. The gas
price these countries face moves from the European hub price towards the LNG price as the share of gas from outside
Russia grows.

$$
gpn^{eus}_t = gpn^{eur}_t\,(1 - s_t) + gpn^{lng}_t\,s_t
$$ {#eq-pr-lng}

where

- $gpn^{eus}_t$ is the gas price of the European market (series `nga.eus`, by source);
- $gpn^{eur}_t$, $gpn^{lng}_t$ are the Europe and LNG series of the same source;
- $s_t$ is the share of gas from outside Russia (Inputs_pint row 3; legacy rows 699, 706).

| Year | before 2022 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 and after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $s_t$ | 0 | 0.58 | 0.603 | 0.734 | 0.834 |

The 2024 value is $1 - (0.303 + 0.229)/2$ and the 2025 value adds 0.1 to it; the share is held from 2025.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Inputs_pint, series `nga.eus` by source, share path in row 3; the country's market from
  Prices_int (Settings C12).
- **CPAT Python:** `prices_data.py`, `EU_LNG` and the last loop of `international_prices()`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
As legacy (LD20, "Same"). The shift was first left out and is now built as legacy's rows 699 and 706.
:::

## Historical domestic prices and forecasting coefficients {#sec-pr-history}

Up to the last historical year the domestic price of each block is data: the IMF price dataset gives the supply cost,
the excise and other taxes, the VAT rate and the retail price. The same data step also sets the coefficients the
projection uses: the pass-through, the fixed part of the supply cost and the VAT rate. The methodology describes the
data in [section 3.2.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PriceHistoricalYears) and
[Appendix C, price reconstruction](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#assumptions-used-for-price-reconstruction-and-projections).

### Supply cost and taxes in the historical years {#sec-pr-history-data}

For each historical year $y$ (data 2021 to $L$):

$$
sp_y = \frac{sp^{n}_y\,\iota_y}{u}, \qquad
txo_y = \frac{\iota_y}{u}\begin{cases} \dfrac{rp^{n}_y}{1 + vatrate_y} - sp^{n}_y & \text{coal, gas, biomass} \\[2mm] txo^{n}_y & \text{oil products} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pr-hist}

where

- $sp^n_y$, $rp^n_y$, $txo^n_y$ are the dataset's supply cost, retail price and excise and other taxes, nominal USD
  per price unit (`mit.sp.<block>`, `mit.rp.<block>`, `mit.txo.<block>`);
- $vatrate_y$ is the VAT rate of the year (below);
- $\iota_y$ is the CPI index of the year and $u$ GJ per price unit ([A2.4](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A2-4)).

So for coal, gas and biomass the taxes are the residual of the dataset's retail price after VAT and supply cost; for
the oil products they are the dataset's own tax column, and the retail price is rebuilt as
$(sp + txo)(1 + vatrate)$, as legacy does.

**Manual values.** Where Settings `DomPrTax` is on, a value typed in the manual price tables replaces the dataset
value for the codes `sp`, `vatrate`, `txo`, `rp` and `pros`. A blank dataset cell reads as 0.

### Pass-through (price controls) {#sec-pr-passthrough}

The **pass-through** $pcc$ says how much of a change in the supply cost reaches the consumer: 1 in a liberalised
market, 0 where the government fixes the retail price. It is set once per block. Settings `GovPriceControls` chooses
how:

| Option | Pass-through |
|---|---|
| *Bucketed* (default) | the dataset's base-year value (`mit.ps.<block>`; blank = 0; biomass 1), bucketed: up to `PassLo` (0.25) → 0; up to `PassHi` (0.5) → `PassMid` (0.5); above → 1 |
| *Manual* | the retail price control of the block from sheet `Manual inputs` J167:J180 (legacy addresses), by the code in column G (`mit.rp.<fuel>.<sector>.ctrl`; legacy default 0.8 for every block); a blank cell gives 1, as legacy rows 747-760. The electricity rows J178:J179 are not read: electricity prices come from @sec-power |
| *None* | 1 for every block |

Egypt, bucketed: coal 1; gas 0; gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene and other oil products 0; biomass 1.

### Fixed part of the supply cost {#sec-pr-fixsp}

The supply cost has a fixed part (margins over the international price and, for coal and gas, the cost of domestic
production) and a part that floats with the international price. The fixed part is set once:

$$
fixsp = \frac{mar\;\iota_{y^m} + dsh\;pcost\;\iota_{t_0}}{u}
$$ {#eq-pr-fixsp}

where

- $fixsp$ is the fixed part of the supply cost (code `spf`, USD/GJ real, constant over the years);
- $mar$ is the margin over international prices (`mit.mar.<block>`, nominal USD per price unit) read in year $y^m$:
  2024 for coal and gas (a typed year, as legacy: issue I101), the base year for the oil products; 0 for biomass;
- $dsh$ is the share of the fuel produced domestically (`mit.coa.prod`, `mit.nga.prod` in the base year, clipped to
  $[0, 1]$; 0 for the other fuels);
- $pcost$ is the domestic production cost (`mit.coa.prod.cost`, `mit.nga.prod.cost`, base year; 0 for the other
  fuels);
- $\iota_{y^m}$, $\iota_{t_0}$ are the CPI indices of the margin year and of the base year.

Other oil products take their pass-through and margin from the dataset like the other oil products (Egypt: 0 and
7.95 USD/bbl).

### VAT rate {#sec-pr-vatrate}

The VAT rate of a block is the dataset's rate where it is filled. Where the cell is blank, consumers pay the general
VAT rate of the country (`VAT_WEO` of the year; Egypt 14%) and firms pay none:

| Block | VAT rate where the data are blank |
|---|---|
| `coa.res`, `nga.res`; `gso.all`, `die.all`, `lpg.all`, `ker.all`, `oop.all` | general rate |
| `coa.pow`, `coa.ind`, `nga.pow`, `nga.ind` | 0 (VAT is credited to firms) |
| `bio.all` | 0 (largely informal) |

The rate used in the projection is the rate of year $L$. For gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene it is then multiplied
by the **household share** of the product (sheet OilProductShares; a blank share counts as 1), because only households
pay VAT on the product; firms reclaim it:

$$
vatrate = vatrate_L \times hsh
$$ {#eq-pr-vatrate}

where $hsh$ is the household share of the oil product (Egypt: gasoline 1, diesel 0.03, LPG 0.99, kerosene 0.39).
Other oil products and the other fuels take the full rate.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: historical prices and coefficients of a block"}
```
for block in PRICES:                              # 12 blocks
    u = gj_per_unit[fuel]
    pcc_raw = 1.0 if fuel == 'bio' else data(t0, 'mit.ps.' + block)
    pcc_bucket = 0 if pcc_raw <= PassLo else (PassMid if pcc_raw <= PassHi else 1)
    pcc = {'Bucketed': pcc_bucket, 'Manual': manual_ctrl[block] or 1, 'None': 1}[GovPriceControls]
    mar_year = 2024 if fuel in ('coa', 'nga') else t0
    mar = 0 if fuel == 'bio' else data(mar_year, 'mit.mar.' + block)
    dsh = clip(data(t0, 'mit.' + fuel + '.prod'), 0, 1) if fuel in ('coa', 'nga') else 0
    pcost = data(t0, 'mit.' + fuel + '.prod.cost') if fuel in ('coa', 'nga') else 0
    spf = (mar * infl[mar_year] + dsh * pcost * infl[t0]) / u
    for y in hist_years:                          # 2021 .. L
        vr_y = data(y, 'mit.vatrate.' + block)
        if blank(vr_y):
            vr_y = VAT_WEO[y] if block in VAT_CONSUMER else 0
        sp[y] = data(y, 'mit.sp.' + block) * infl[y] / u
        if fuel in ('coa', 'nga', 'bio'):
            txo[y] = (data(y, 'mit.rp.' + block) / (1 + vr_y) - data(y, 'mit.sp.' + block)) * infl[y] / u
        else:
            txo[y] = data(y, 'mit.txo.' + block) * infl[y] / u
    vr = vr_L * (household_share[fuel] if block in OIL_SHARE else 1)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Inputs_prices (`build_inputs_prices`; Inputs rows 158-169) from sheet Prices_dom (or the manual
  tables where `DomPrTax` is on); Settings `GovPriceControls`, `PassLo`, `PassMid`, `PassHi`; sheet `Manual inputs`
  J167:J180; sheet OilProductShares.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/prices_data.py`, `domestic_prices()` and `DomesticData`; equation A2.4.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD2 (decision), L13.** Legacy hardcodes the pass-through of other oil products to 1 and their margin to 0. The
  model takes both from the dataset. Under the legacy rule their retail price fell with the oil price to the 0.01
  floor (3.79 USD/GJ in 2024, 0.23 in 2030) and their fuel use rose tenfold by 2030.
- **LD3 (VAT where the data are blank).** The general VAT rate for residential coal and gas and the all-sector oil
  products; 0 for power, industry and biomass. Only blank cells are filled (user decision).
- **LD5, issue I39 (household share).** VAT on gasoline, diesel, LPG and kerosene is charged on the household share
  only, as legacy rows 797-816.
- **LD16, L172 (margins and production cost in real terms).** Legacy adds the margin and the production cost in
  nominal USD to real prices. The model converts each with the CPI index of the year it is read.
- **LD80 (production-cost weight, as legacy).** The production cost is weighted by the share produced domestically
  (legacy P747:P752), not by the bucketed pass-through (an earlier prototype rule).
- **I101.** Coal and gas margins are read at the typed year 2024, as legacy.
- **LD4, I150 (Egypt data).** The Egypt price data equal legacy's cell by cell, except the spot coal and gas cells,
  which legacy 465 fills with a year and 0; the model keeps the module values (no effect unless the spot option is
  chosen).
- **I89 (price vintage).** The last historical price year is 2024, as legacy 456/465 (price data through 2024,
  projection from 2025).
:::

## Producer subsidies {#sec-pr-producer}

A producer subsidy lowers the cost at which a fuel is supplied, so it sits inside the supply cost, before any tax. The
dataset gives each producer subsidy as a total amount; the model spreads it over the demand that carries it, to get a
subsidy per unit. The methodology treats producer subsidies as part of the supply price
([section 3.2.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PricesForecastedYears)).

**Amount.** For each producer fuel (coal, gas, oil, biomass, electricity):

$$
pros_{f,t} = \begin{cases} PROS^{n}_{f,t}\;\iota_t \times 1000 & t \le L \\ pros_{f,t-1} & t > L \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pr-pros}

where $pros_{f,t}$ is the producer subsidy before the phase-out (USD million real) and $PROS^n_{f,t}$ the dataset
value (`mit.pros.<fuel>.all`, USD billion nominal, or a manual value).

**Demand that carries it.** The subsidy is spread over:

| Fuel | Demand $D_f$ (code `psd`) | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Oil | world demand × liters per ktoe (1,108,792) | liters |
| Coal | average of world demand and domestic consumption × GJ per ktoe (41,868) | GJ |
| Gas | average of world demand and domestic consumption × GJ per ktoe | GJ |
| Biomass | domestic consumption × GJ per ktoe | GJ |

World demand is the global production of the fuel in the IEA scenario chosen by `GlobalEnergyDemand` (stated
policies, announced pledges or sustainable development; Mtoe × 1000). Domestic consumption is the energy use of the
fuel in sheet EnergyCons, excluding electricity output and international bunkers.

**Per unit, after the phase-out.**

$$
psu_{f,t} = \begin{cases} -\dfrac{pros_{f,t} \times 10^6}{D_{f,t}} & t \le L \\[2mm] psu_{f,L}\;psf_{f,t} & t > L \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pr-psu}

where

- $psu_{f,t}$ is the producer subsidy per unit after the phase-out (negative; USD per liter for oil, USD/GJ for coal,
  gas and biomass);
- $psf_{f,t}$ is the producer subsidy factor of the fuel: the share of the subsidy kept (@eq-pr-incl; 1 without a
  reform).

**Per block.** Each block reads the subsidy of its international-price commodity and converts it to USD/GJ:

$$
ps_{g,f,t} = \frac{psu_{m(f),t} \times (\text{liters per barrel if } f = \text{oop})}{u}
$$ {#eq-pr-ps}

where $m(f)$ is oil for the five oil products, coal, gas, or biomass, and liters per barrel = 158.987. The producer
subsidy enters the supply cost (@eq-pr-sp), so its phase-out raises the supply cost; the floating taxes then absorb
$(1 - pcc)$ of the rise, as for any other change in the supply cost
([A2.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A2-5)).

The fiscal cost of producer subsidies after the phase-out, $-\sum_f pros_f\,psf_f$ (code `rpsu`), is in the revenue
totals (@sec-fiscal). The electricity producer subsidy is allocated in the power module (@sec-power). Egypt has no
producer subsidy data, so $ps = 0$.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: producer subsidies"}
```
for f in ['coa', 'nga', 'oil', 'bio', 'ecy']:
    for t in years:
        pros[f][t] = data(t, 'mit.pros.' + f + '.all') * infl[t] * 1000 if t <= L else pros[f][t-1]
for f in ['oil', 'coa', 'nga', 'bio']:
    for t in years:
        psd[f][t] = {'oil': world[f][t] * 1000 * LitersPerKtoeOil,
                     'coa': (world[f][t] * 1000 + cons[f]) / 2 * GJperKtoe,
                     'nga': (world[f][t] * 1000 + cons[f]) / 2 * GJperKtoe,
                     'bio': cons[f] * GJperKtoe}[f]
        psu[f][t] = -pros[f][t] * 1e6 / psd[f][t] if t <= L else psu[f][L] * psf[f][t]
for block in PRICES:
    for t in years:
        ps[block][t] = psu[commodity[block]][t] * (LitersPerBbl if fuel == 'oop' else 1) / u[block]
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation section 1 rows `pros`, `psd`, `psu` (Formulas E150-E152), section 2 row `ps`
  (E246); revenue row `rpsu` (E1051, section 12).
- **CPAT Python:** `prices.py`, `prepare()` (producer subsidies), `world_demand()`, `domestic_use()`; equation A2.5.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD19, I49 (as legacy).** Producer subsidies are spread over world or domestic demand and kept in the supply cost
  (legacy rows 825-829 and the "in which: producer-side subsidies" rows 2455-2708); the phase-out multiplies the
  per-unit subsidy by the factor, as legacy O2455 = J2456 × O2213. Earlier prototype versions held them as a fiscal
  line only, then as a separate wedge (`psw`, `ppsw`, `psr`; removed).
- **L124, L82 (fixed).** Legacy's residential gas block reads the oil producer subsidy.
- **L125 (fixed).** Legacy's other oil products add a per-liter subsidy to a per-barrel price.
:::

## Supply cost {#sec-pr-supply}

After the last historical year the supply cost moves with the international price. Only its floating part moves: the
fixed part (margins, production cost) stays, and the producer subsidy is added back at its current level.

$$
sp_{t} = fixsp + \left(sp_{t-1} - fixsp - ps_{t-1}\right)\frac{gp_t}{gp_{t-1}} + ps_t, \qquad t > L
$$ {#eq-pr-sp}

where

- $sp_t$ is the supply cost of the block (code `sp`, USD/GJ real; data up to $L$, @eq-pr-hist);
- $fixsp$ is its fixed part (@eq-pr-fixsp);
- $gp_t$ is the block's international reference price (`gpi`, @eq-pr-gp);
- $ps_t$ is the producer subsidy of the block (@eq-pr-ps).

This is the equation list's [M2.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-1). The methodology writes it as three parts,
$sp = fixsp + fltsp + ps$ with $fltsp_t = fltsp_{t-1}\,gp_t / gp_{t-1}$
([Appendix C, calculations](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#calculations-modeling-assumptions));
the model's equation is the same with $fltsp_{t-1} = sp_{t-1} - fixsp - ps_{t-1}$.

Biomass has a flat international price, so its supply cost stays at its value of year $L$.

## Excise and other taxes: pass-through {#sec-pr-txo}

The excise and other taxes `txo` are the net of every existing tax and consumer subsidy other than VAT. Their
projection carries the **price control**: the share of a supply-cost change that is not passed through is absorbed by
the taxes (or by the subsidy, which then floats). The methodology calls this the floating portion of taxes and
subsidies ([Appendix C, price liberalization](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#price-liberalization)).

**Floating taxes.** Each year the taxes absorb $(1 - pcc)$ of the change in the supply cost:

$$
\widetilde{txo}_t = \widetilde{txo}_{t-1} - \left(sp_t - sp_{t-1}\right)\left(1 - pcc\right), \qquad \widetilde{txo}_t = txo_t \text{ for } t \le L
$$ {#eq-pr-txf}

which adds up to $\widetilde{txo}_t = txo_L + (sp_L - sp_t)(1 - pcc)$
([M2.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-2)).

**Floor on a positive tax.** A tax that was positive in year $L$ does not fall below that level; a subsidy floats
freely:

$$
txo_t = \begin{cases} \max\left(txo_L,\ \widetilde{txo}_t\right) & txo_L \ge 0 \\ \widetilde{txo}_t & txo_L < 0 \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pr-txo}

where $\widetilde{txo}_t$ is the floating value (code `txf`) and $txo_t$ the excise and other taxes before new
policies (code `txo`, USD/GJ real; [A2.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A2-1)).

The two extreme cases make the rule clear:

- **$pcc = 1$ (liberalised).** Supply-cost changes are passed on in full; the taxes stay at $txo_L$.
- **$pcc = 0$ (fixed price).** The price before new policies stays at its value of year $L$; the subsidy (or the tax)
  absorbs every change in the supply cost. For Egypt's gas and oil products, a fall in the oil price shrinks the
  subsidy and a rise widens it.

Here `txo` holds existing taxes and subsidies only. The methodology's $txo$ also holds the existing and new carbon
prices and the new excise; the model keeps those apart as wedges (@sec-pr-ecp, @sec-pr-atp).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **L14 (fixed).** With a pass-through of 0.5 or 0.8, legacy applies $(1 - pcc)$ twice in the first projected year
  (the floating subsidy is multiplied by $(1 - pcc)$ a second time), so other taxes jump. The model applies it once.
  No effect for Egypt (pass-through 0 or 1).
- **Methodology.** The methodology averages the fixed and floating portions over five historical years (2018-2022)
  and multiplies the floating part by the price-control phase-out factor. The model, as legacy, projects from the
  single year $L$ and keeps the phase-out as a separate wedge (@sec-pr-phaseouts).
:::

## VAT, the price before new policies and existing taxes {#sec-pr-pbc}

VAT is charged on the supply cost plus the other taxes. With it the block reaches its **retail price before new
policies**, the price a consumer would pay if no new policy were introduced.

$$
vat_t = \left(sp_t + txo_t\right) vatrate, \qquad p^{0}_t = \left(sp_t + txo_t\right)\left(1 + vatrate\right)
$$ {#eq-pr-pbc}

where

- $vat_t$ is the VAT payment before new policies (code `vat`, USD/GJ real);
- $vatrate$ is the block's VAT rate (@eq-pr-vatrate; code `vr` in CPAT Python);
- $p^0_t$ is the retail price before new policies (code `pbc`; [M2.3](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-3)).

**Existing taxes and subsidies.** The net `txo` is split by sign, so that taxes and subsidies can be reported and
reformed separately. Subsidies are negative throughout the model.

| Item | Code | Formula | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| VAT before new policies | `vat` | $(sp + txo)\,vatrate$ | VAT revenue |
| Existing excise and other taxes | `etx` | $\max(txo, 0)$ | existing-tax revenue |
| Existing consumer subsidy | `esub` | $\min(txo, 0)$ | existing subsidies (negative) |
| Subsidy per price unit | `esubpu` | $esub \times u$ | in ScenarioDefinition price units (USD/liter, USD/bbl, USD/GJ), the units of the fuel price reform inputs, so a per-fuel subsidy reform can be typed there |
| Fixed part of `txo` | `fadtx` | $pcc \times txo_t$ for $t \le L$; $pcc \times txo_L$ after | the part that does not float; subsidy reform (@sec-pr-phaseouts) |
| Floating part of `txo` | `cs` | $txo - fadtx$ | absorbs the supply-cost changes not passed through; price-control phase-out |

Revenue at these rates (fuel use in PJ × the rate) is in @sec-fiscal: existing taxes = excise + VAT + the change in
existing carbon pricing with its VAT; existing subsidies = the subsidy (negative); net existing = taxes + subsidies.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: the build-up of a block before new policies"}
```
for block in PRICES:
    txf[:L], txo[:L] = txo_hist, txo_hist        # data years
    for t in years after L:
        sp[t] = spf + (sp[t-1] - spf - ps[t-1]) * gpi[t] / gpi[t-1] + ps[t]
        txf[t] = txf[t-1] - (sp[t] - sp[t-1]) * (1 - pcc)
        txo[t] = max(txo[L], txf[t]) if txo[L] >= 0 else txf[t]
    for t in years:
        fadtx[t] = pcc * (txo[t] if t <= L else txo[L])
        cs[t] = txo[t] - fadtx[t]
        etx[t], esub[t] = max(txo[t], 0), min(txo[t], 0)
        esubpu[t] = esub[t] * u
        vat[t] = (sp[t] + txo[t]) * vr
        pbc[t] = (sp[t] + txo[t]) * (1 + vr)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation section 2 rows `spf`, `ps`, `sp`, `txf`, `txo`, `fadtx`, `cs`, `etx`, `esub`,
  `esubpu`, `vat`, `pbc` (Formulas E244-E255).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/prices.py`, `prepare()` (the loop over `pdx.PRICES`); equations M2.1-M2.3,
  A2.1.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD17 (Same), LD14 (decision).** Legacy splits `txo` into a fixed tax, a fixed subsidy and a floating part; the
  model splits it by sign, which gives the same totals. Subsidies are negative (`esub`, `esubpu`, `rsub`).
- **L60 (fixed).** Legacy computes the VAT payment of oil products by dividing the retail price by 1 + the full VAT
  rate; the model uses $(sp + txo) \times$ rate $\times$ household share.
- **Ad-valorem taxes.** Legacy reads a per-country ad-valorem flag for baseline taxes (Prices_int H, Mitigation F77)
  but no formula uses it: taxes are fixed in both (LD20).
:::

## Subsidy and price-control phase-outs {#sec-pr-phaseouts}

Two reforms remove the existing consumer support. The **consumer subsidy reform** removes the fixed subsidy; the
**price-control phase-out** (price liberalisation) removes the floating part, so the consumer comes to pay the
supply-cost changes. Both are separate policy lines, by price block: the price before new policies `pbc` is not
changed, and the reforms are wedges added to the after-tax price like the new policies. The methodology describes them
in [Appendix C, fossil fuel subsidies reform](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#fossil-fuel-subsidies-reform)
and [price liberalization](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#price-liberalization).

### Phase-out factors {#sec-pr-pof}

There is one factor per reform $k$: producer subsidies (`ps`), consumer subsidies (`cs`) and price controls (`pc`).
Each is the share of the original support still kept, the same in every year for every line:

$$
pof_{k,t} = \begin{cases} \max\!\left(1 - \bar{s}_k,\ 1 - \bar{s}_k\,\dfrac{t - T_k}{\max(N_k, 1)}\right) & \text{the reform is on and } t > T_k \\[2mm] 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pr-pof}

where

- $pof_{k,t}$ is the phase-out factor (code `pof`; [M1.7](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M1-7));
- $\bar{s}_k$ is the share to phase out (`po.sh`), $T_k$ the start year and $N_k$ the period in years (`po.n`).

The inputs come from ScenarioDefinition. Scenario 1 reads the baseline switch, period and share; the other scenarios
read the policy switch and period, with the share the larger of the baseline and the policy share (legacy rows
264-274). The price-control phase-out applies only if its policy switch is on and either the scenario is a policy
scenario or its baseline switch is on. It uses the consumer-subsidy shares (issue I48) and the same period in every
scenario. A switch counts as on if it is TRUE or starts with "Yes".

| Reform | Switch (policy / baseline) | Start year | Period (policy / baseline) | Share (policy / baseline) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Producer subsidies | `ProdSubPh` / `ProdSubPhaBaseline` | `YearProdSubPha` | `FFSProdPhaseoutPeriod` / `FFSProdPhaseoutPeriodBA` | `ShareofProdSubPha` / `ShareOfProdSubPhaBA` |
| Consumer subsidies | `ConsSubPha` / `ConsSubPhaBaseline` | `YearConsSubPha` | `FFPhaseOut` / `FFSConsPhaseoutPeriodBA` | `ShareOfConsSubPha` / `ShareofConsSubPhaBA` |
| Price controls | `PrcContPha` / `PrcContPhaBaseline` | `YearPrcContPha` | `PrcControlPhaseout` (both) | the consumer shares |

: Phase-out inputs (ScenarioDefinition rows 123-137 and 191-195) {#tbl-pr-pof}

**Which blocks and fuels a reform covers.** Inclusion switches on ScenarioDefinition, per scenario, let a reform cover
some fuels and sectors only: `ConsSubPhaseScope_<block>` ($csi$) and `PriceCtrlPhaseScope_<block>` ($pci$) for the
12 price blocks, and `ProdSubPhaseScope_<fuel>` ($psi$) for coal, gas, oil, biomass and electricity. Each turns the
reform factor into the factor of its line:

$$
csf = 1 - csi\,(1 - pof_{cs}), \qquad pcf = 1 - pci\,(1 - pof_{pc}), \qquad psf_f = 1 - psi_f\,(1 - pof_{ps})
$$ {#eq-pr-incl}

### The wedges {#sec-pr-wedges}

Each block splits its taxes into the fixed part `fadtx` and the floating part `cs` (@sec-pr-pbc). The consumer
subsidy reform removes the share $(1 - csf)$ of a fixed subsidy; the price-control phase-out removes the share
$(1 - pcf)$ of the floating part, whether that is a subsidy or a tax:

$$
pcsw_t = -\left(1 - csf_t\right)\min\left(fadtx_t,\ 0\right), \qquad
ppcw_t = -\left(1 - pcf_t\right) cs_t
$$ {#eq-pr-wedges}

where

- $pcsw_t$ is the consumer subsidy reform wedge of the block (USD/GJ, before VAT);
- $ppcw_t$ is the price-control phase-out wedge of the block (USD/GJ, before VAT).

Because the two wedges act on different parts of `txo`, using both reforms does not count a subsidy twice. For Egypt
every subsidised fuel has pass-through 0, so its whole subsidy floats: only the price-control phase-out removes it, as
in legacy.

Every subsector reads the wedges of its block as `csw` and `pcw` and adds them, with VAT, to its after-tax price
(@eq-pr-atp). The revenue of the reforms, $F\,\theta\,(csw + pcw)(1 + vatrate)$ (code `rsr`: the subsidy saved plus the
VAT on it), and the producer-subsidy line `rpsu` are in @sec-fiscal; the net existing revenue `rnet` stays the
pre-reform one.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: phase-outs and wedges"}
```
for k in ['ps', 'cs', 'pc']:
    on, start, period, share = phaseout_inputs(k, scenario)    # baseline or policy columns
    for t in years:
        pof[k][t] = max(1 - share, 1 - share * (t - start) / max(period, 1)) if on and t > start else 1
for block in PRICES:
    for t in years:
        csf[block][t] = 1 - csi[block] * (1 - pof['cs'][t])
        pcf[block][t] = 1 - pci[block] * (1 - pof['pc'][t])
        pcsw[block][t] = -(1 - csf[block][t]) * min(fadtx[block][t], 0)
        ppcw[block][t] = -(1 - pcf[block][t]) * cs[block][t]
for f in ['coa', 'nga', 'oil', 'bio', 'ecy']:
    for t in years:
        psf[f][t] = 1 - psi[f] * (1 - pof['ps'][t])
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation section 1 rows `po.on`, `po.n`, `po.sh`, `pof`, `csi`, `csf`, `pci`, `pcf`, `psi`,
  `psf` (Formulas E140-E149); section 2 rows `pcsw`, `ppcw` (E261, E262); subsector rows `csw`, `pcw` (E454, E455).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/policies.py`, `prepare()` (phase-outs, equation M1.7); `prices.py`,
  `prepare()` (`pcsw`, `ppcw`); `fuel_use.py`, `prepare()` (`csw`, `pcw`).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD18 (as legacy, user decision).** Separate policy lines, not meshed with the pre-policy build-up: `sp`, `txo` and
  `pbc` are unchanged and the reforms are wedges. Legacy multiplies the fixed subsidy and the floating part by the
  factors inside its price rows (legacy rows 2597-2599 of each block, 2211-2218 for the factors); the prices are the
  same.
- **L81 (fixed).** Legacy lags the consumer phase-out of the fixed subsidy by a year; the model uses the same year
  for every line.
- **I48 (replicated).** The price-control phase-out uses the consumer-subsidy share.
- **Methodology note.** The methodology advises not to combine price liberalisation with the subsidy phase-out to
  avoid double counting; in the model the two act on disjoint parts of `txo`.
:::

## Existing carbon pricing {#sec-pr-ecp}

Some countries already price carbon, with a carbon tax, a national ETS or the EU ETS. The IMF retail prices already
contain whatever existing carbon pricing a country had, so the model adds only the **change** against that level:
growth after the last data year, new data, or a scheme switched off. A country's history is never counted twice. The
methodology describes existing carbon pricing in
[section 3.2.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PricesForecastedYears) and
[Appendix C, policy options](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#policy-options-existing-carbon-pricing-policies).

### Data and tables {#sec-pr-ecp-data}

The data are the World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard and ICAP data of sheet ECP (as of 1 April 2025; 52 countries;
Egypt has none), read at their legacy addresses. Each code is looked up in its own legacy block (sheet Inputs_ecp,
columns K:L give each block's first and last row):

| Scheme | Codes | Legacy rows of sheet ECP |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon tax | single rate `ecr.all`, fuel rates `ecr.<fuel>`, sector coverage `ecs.<sector>`, fuel coverage `ecf.<fuel>` | 69-559 |
| National ETS | price `eer.all`, coverage `ees.<sector>`, `eef.<fuel>` | 600-615, 619-737, 1040-1093 |
| EU ETS (regional) | the EU price (row 616), the country's regional coverage | 738-1036, 1094-1223 |

- Prices are made real with the CPI index of the data year.
- Coverage is that of each data year (2021-2025; blank = 0, as legacy); the last data year holds after it.
- The carbon tax rate of a fuel is the fuel rate where the country has one and no "single price" flag (general
  information, column E); otherwise the single rate (legacy rows 1752-1764).
- The EU ETS counts where the country's "EU ETS?" flag (general information, column K) is Yes or Both (legacy row 1695).

From these the model builds two tables by ECP sector $j$ (power, transport, buildings, industry), fuel $f$ and data
year $y$, in USD/tCO2:

$$
XT_{j,f,y} = rate_{f,y}\;scov_{j,y}\;fcov_{f,y}, \qquad
XE_{j,f,y} = p^{nat}_y\;ncov_{j,y}\;nfcov_{f,y} + p^{EU}_y\;rcov_{j,y}\;rfcov_{f,y}
$$ {#eq-pr-ecptables}

where $XT$ is the existing carbon tax and $XE$ the existing ETS price of the sector and fuel. The national and the EU
schemes add up, as legacy. Existing coverage is fractional; coverage of the new policies is a yes/no switch.

**ECP sector of a price.** Coal and gas take their price sector (power, residential, industry); the oil products,
biomass and jet fuel take transport; other oil products take industry; power takes power.

### Factors, level and change {#sec-pr-ecp-change}

ScenarioDefinition decides, per scenario, whether each scheme applies and how its real price grows after the last
data year $T_x$ (2025):

$$
\varphi^{ct}_t = \mathbb{1}[\texttt{ExistingCTApply}]\,(1 + \gamma^{ct})^{\max(0,\,t - T_x)}, \qquad
\varphi^{ets}_t = \mathbb{1}[\texttt{ExistingETSApply}]\,(1 + \gamma^{ets})^{\max(0,\,t - T_x)}
$$ {#eq-pr-ecpfactor}

where $\gamma^{ct}$ is `ExistingCTGrowth` and $\gamma^{ets}$ is `ExistingETSGrowth` (real growth per year; codes
`xct.p`, `xets.p`).

Then, per subsector and fuel:

$$
xcp_{s,f,t} = ef_{s,f}\left(XT_{j,f,t^*}\,\varphi^{ct}_t + XE_{j,f,t^*}\,\varphi^{ets}_t\right), \qquad
\Delta xcp_{s,f,t} = xcp_{s,f,t} - ef_{s,f}\,XCP^{0}_{j,f}
$$ {#eq-pr-xcp}

where

- $xcp_{s,f,t}$ is the level of existing carbon pricing (code `xcp`, USD/GJ);
- $\Delta xcp_{s,f,t}$ is its change against the price data (code `xcpd`, USD/GJ;
  [A2.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A2-2));
- $ef_{s,f}$ is the calibrated CO2 emission factor (tCO2/GJ; @sec-emissions);
- $t^* = \min(t, T_x)$ is the data column of the year (code `xct.c`), $j = j(s,f)$ the ECP sector;
- $XCP^0_{j,f} = XT_{j,f,y_e} + XE_{j,f,y_e}$ is the existing carbon pricing embedded in the price data, the tables in
  the year $y_e = \min(L, T_x)$ (2024).

Only $\Delta xcp$ enters the after-tax price (@eq-pr-atp). Switching a scheme off therefore lowers the price by its
embedded level; growth or new data raise it.

**Power.** The same change per kWh (the power row of the tables) is part of the variable cost before new policies,
so dispatch, investment and electricity prices respond (@sec-power).

**New carbon tax beside an existing ETS.** If `CTaxComplimentaryToETS` = Yes (legacy rows 2270-2288), the new carbon
tax of a sector covers 1 − the national ETS sector coverage of the year (@sec-model-overview). Otherwise new
instruments add to existing ones.

**Revenue.** The existing-tax revenue includes $\Delta xcp\,(1 + vatrate)$; a memo shows the level, fuel use ×
$xcp$. Existing ETS revenue is valued at the full permit price, as legacy; legacy's free-allocation and revenue data
(ECP rows 560-597, 1225-1322) are not used, in legacy's model either (@sec-fiscal).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: existing carbon pricing"}
```
Tx = 2025                                         # last ECP data year
y_e = min(L, Tx)                                  # year embedded in the price data
for t in years:
    col = min(t, Tx)
    xct_p[t] = (1 + ExistingCTGrowth) ** max(0, t - Tx) if ExistingCTApply == 'Yes' else 0
    xets_p[t] = (1 + ExistingETSGrowth) ** max(0, t - Tx) if ExistingETSApply == 'Yes' else 0
for s in subsectors:
    for f in fuels:
        j = ecp_sector(s, f)
        xcp0 = XT[j, f, y_e] + XE[j, f, y_e]
        for t in years:
            level = XT[j, f, col] * xct_p[t] + XE[j, f, col] * xets_p[t]
            xcp[s, f, t] = ef[s, f] * level
            xcpd[s, f, t] = ef[s, f] * (level - xcp0)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet ECP (data), sheet Inputs_ecp (tables `XCTVal`, `XETSVal`; Inputs rows 611-739); sheet
  Mitigation section 1 rows `xct.c`, `xct.p`, `xets.p` (Formulas E119-E121); subsector rows `xcp`, `xcpd` (E452,
  E453). Inputs: ScenarioDefinition `ExistingCTApply`, `ExistingCTGrowth`, `ExistingETSApply`,
  `ExistingETSGrowth`, `CTaxComplimentaryToETS` (MTInputs rows 208-214).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/policies.py`, `ecp_table()`, `ecp_embedded_year()` and `prepare()`
  (factors); `fuel_data.fuel_table()` (`ecpk`, `xcp0`); `fuel_use.py`, `prepare()` (`xcp`, `xcpd`); equation A2.2.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD38.** Legacy adds existing carbon taxes and ETS from its sheet ECP as parts of `txo` (Mitigation rows
  1675-1764, 1711-1723 for the ETS, 1752-1764 for the tax). The model follows legacy with several schemes (user
  decision 2026-10-18), but adds only the change against the level in the price data; legacy subtracts the same level
  from the fixed part of `txo`, which gives the same numbers.
- **L61 (fixed).** Legacy grows the EU ETS price with the carbon-tax growth.
- **L62 (fixed).** Legacy's transport diesel, LPG and kerosene take the rate row as coverage.
- **L63 (fixed).** Legacy's fuel-coverage lookup stops at row 403 of a block that ends at 425.
- **L64 (fixed).** Legacy has no ETS on other oil products outside power.
- **L65 (fixed).** Legacy's complementary new tax uses the previous year's ETS coverage.
- **Methodology.** The methodology grows the existing price from the base year $t_0$; the model uses the data of each
  year to 2025 and grows it from there.
:::

## New policies and the after-tax price {#sec-pr-atp}

The new policies of a scenario act per subsector and fuel, because coverage, exemptions and emission factors differ
by subsector. Each policy is turned into a cost per GJ and added, with VAT, to the price before new policies of the
subsector's block. The result is the **after-tax price**, the price that drives fuel use. The methodology describes
the new carbon price and the new excise in
[section 3.2.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PricesForecastedYears) and in
[Appendix C, policy coverage and exemptions](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#policy-coverage-and-exemptions).

### New carbon tax, ETS cost and excise per GJ {#sec-pr-new}

$$
nct_{s,f} = NCT_s\;ef_{s,f}\;\varphi_{NCT,f}\;x_{s,f}, \qquad
netsp_{s,f} = NETSP_s\;ef_{s,f}\;x_{s,f}, \qquad
nexc_{s,f} = \frac{F^{x}_{c(s,f)}}{u_f}\;x_{s,f}
$$ {#eq-pr-new}

where

- $nct_{s,f}$, $netsp_{s,f}$, $nexc_{s,f}$ are the new carbon tax, the new ETS cost and the new excise (codes
  `ctxnew`, `ets`, `ntx`; USD/GJ; [M2.4](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-4));
- $NCT_s$ is the new carbon tax rate of the sector (USD/tCO2; code `ctr`): the explicit carbon price where the sector
  is covered and not in a new ETS (@sec-model-overview);
- $NETSP_s$ is the ETS cost in the price of the sector (code `etr`): the tax-equivalent permit price × ETS coverage ×
  the auctioned share (@sec-emissions);
- $ef_{s,f}$ is the calibrated CO2 emission factor (tCO2/GJ);
- $\varphi_{NCT,f}$ is the carbon-tax coverage of the fuel (code `ctcov`: 1 if covered, else the exemption phase-out
  path; biomass is covered with emission factor 0);
- $F^x_c$ is the new excise of the price fuel $c(s,f)$ in price units (code `ntxb`; @eq-pr-ntxb), and $u_f$ GJ per
  price unit of the fuel row;
- $x_{s,f}$ is the exemption factor (code `exf`, below).

**The new excise.** The fuel price reform path `fpr` (@sec-model-overview, [M1.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M1-5)) is
set per price fuel in price units (USD/liter, USD/bbl, USD/GJ). It acts **only in the policy scenarios**:

$$
F^x_{c,t} = \mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\;ntxg_{c,t}, \qquad ntxg_{c,t} = fpr_{c,t} + \mathbb{1}[\texttt{AddEfficientTaxes}]\;pigx_{c,t}
$$ {#eq-pr-ntxb}

where $ntxg$ is the gross new excise (code `ntxg`) and $pigx$ the Pigouvian tax (@sec-pr-pigou; with
`AddEfficientTaxes` = Yes the formula of $F^x$ changes, @eq-pr-pigntx). Jet fuel reads the kerosene reform per
liter and divides it by its own GJ per liter.

**Total new policy:**

$$
nce_{s,f} = nct_{s,f} + netsp_{s,f} + nexc_{s,f}
$$ {#eq-pr-nce}

**Residential LPG and kerosene always exempted.** ScenarioDefinition `AlwaysExemptResLPGKer` (row 268, by scenario;
default No*) exempts these two rows from every new policy. If the switch starts with "Yes" (Yes or Yes*), the
exemption factor of the residential LPG and kerosene rows is 0; every other row has factor 1:

$$
x_{s,f} = \begin{cases} 0 & f \in \{\text{LPG, kerosene}\},\ s = \text{residential},\ \texttt{AlwaysExemptResLPGKer} \text{ starts with "Yes"} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-pr-exf}

Their new carbon tax, ETS cost and new excise are then 0, so neither is the VAT on them, nor their new-policy revenue
(`rnew`, the excise revenue `rex` and the VAT on new policies in `rvt`). Existing taxes, the change in existing
carbon pricing and the subsidy phase-outs stay, as legacy (row 2651, the price before new policies). The shadow price
is not exempted, as legacy. ETS-covered emissions still count them where the residential sector is in an ETS
(@sec-emissions), and the residential leakage to biomass reads the row's own `nce`, so an exempt fuel does not leak
(@sec-demand).

### The after-tax price {#sec-pr-atp-eq}

$$
p_{s,f} = \max\!\Big(p^{0}_{g,f} + \big(nce_{s,f} + \Delta xcp_{s,f} + csw_{s,f} + pcw_{s,f}\big)\left(1 + vatrate_{g,f}\right),\ \underline{p}\Big)
$$ {#eq-pr-atp}

where

- $p_{s,f}$ is the after-tax price of fuel $f$ in subsector $s$ (code `atp`, USD/GJ real;
  [M2.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-5));
- $g$ is the price sector of $(s,f)$, so $p^0_{g,f}$ is the price before new policies of the block (@eq-pr-pbc) and
  $vatrate_{g,f}$ its VAT rate;
- $\Delta xcp_{s,f}$ is the change in existing carbon pricing (@eq-pr-xcp);
- $csw_{s,f}$, $pcw_{s,f}$ are the subsidy and price-control wedges of the block (@eq-pr-wedges);
- $\underline{p}$ is the price floor (`PriceFloor`, 0.01 USD/GJ, legacy's).

New policies are passed through in full and pay VAT, as legacy's VAT on `txo` with `nce` inside it. With the
exemption, the residential LPG and kerosene price is
$\max(p^0 + (\Delta xcp + csw + pcw)(1 + vatrate), \underline{p})$.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: new policies and the after-tax price"}
```
for c in price_fuels_14:                         # 12 blocks + ecy.res, ecy.ind
    for t in years:
        ntxg[c][t] = fpr[c][t] + (pigx[c][t] if AddEfficientTaxes == 'Yes' else 0)
        ntxb[c][t] = ntxg[c][t] if scenario > 1 else 0          # (Pigouvian netting: see below)
for s in subsectors:
    for f in fuels:
        block = price_block(s, f)                # e.g. ('nga', 'res') for road gas
        x = exf['res'] if (s, f) in [('res', 'lpg'), ('res', 'ker')] else exf['all']
        for t in years:
            ctxnew[s, f, t] = ctr[s][t] * ef[s, f] * ctcov[f][t] * x
            ets[s, f, t] = etr[s][t] * ef[s, f] * x
            ntx[s, f, t] = ntxb[price_fuel(s, f)][t] / u[f] * x
            nce[s, f, t] = ctxnew[s, f, t] + ets[s, f, t] + ntx[s, f, t]
            csw[s, f, t], pcw[s, f, t] = pcsw[block][t], ppcw[block][t]
            atp[s, f, t] = max(pbc[block][t]
                               + (nce[s, f, t] + xcpd[s, f, t] + csw[s, f, t] + pcw[s, f, t]) * (1 + vr[block]),
                               PriceFloor)
            shp[s, f, t] = shpx[s][t] * ef[s, f]
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation section 1 rows `fpr` (E28), `ntxg` (E54), `ntxb` (E57), `exf` (E157); subsector
  rows of sections 5-8: `ctxnew`, `ets`, `ntx`, `nce`, `xcp`, `xcpd`, `csw`, `pcw`, `atp`, `shp` (Formulas
  E448-E457). Lookups on sheet Inputs (rows 5-148): emission factor W, fuel position L, sector position M, price-fuel
  position N, GJ per unit K, price position U, VAT rate V, exemption group BE. Inputs: ScenarioDefinition
  `AlwaysExemptResLPGKer` (row 268), sheet Constants `exf|all|all`, `PriceFloor`.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/policies.py`, `prepare()` (`fpr`, `ntxg`, `ntxb`, `exf`);
  `fuel_use.py`, `prepare()` (the price rows of every fuel block); equations M2.4, M2.5, M2.6.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **Legacy structure.** Legacy keeps the new carbon tax, ETS cost and excise inside `txo` (legacy Mitigation rows
  2510, 2512, 2514); the model keeps them as separate rows and adds them with VAT, which gives the same price.
- **Exemption (legacy rows 5546-5547).** Legacy: IF(`AlwaysExemptResLPGKer` = "Yes", 0, new policy × coverage). The
  model reads the first three letters, so a starred "Yes*" also counts.
- **LD57.** The new carbon tax and ETS cost use the calibrated emission factors (@sec-emissions).
- **LD10, L171, L173 (fixed).** The fuel price reform path holds the target level after the target year under option
  No (legacy drops it to 0), and its Percentage continuation grows at (1 + rate) (legacy multiplies by the rate).
:::

## The shadow price {#sec-pr-shadow}

Some policies change behaviour without changing what consumers pay: feebates, efficiency regulations and the part of
a new ETS that is allocated free. The model represents them as a **shadow price** per GJ. Demand responds to it on the
efficiency margin only, and it raises no revenue.

$$
sh_{s,f} = \Sigma_s\;ef_{s,f}
$$ {#eq-pr-shp}

where

- $sh_{s,f}$ is the shadow price per GJ (code `shp`; [M2.6](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-6));
- $\Sigma_s$ is the shadow price of sector $s$ per tonne (code `shpx`;
  [M1.4](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M1-4)): the feebate rate × the share of the feebate on the efficiency margin, plus the
  shadow price of regulations, plus the tax-equivalent ETS price × ETS coverage × the share allocated free
  (@sec-model-overview).

The demand equation uses the after-tax price twice: alone in the usage term, and with the shadow price in the
efficiency term, $\big((p + sh)_t / (p + sh)_{t-1}\big)^{\varepsilon_F (1 + \varepsilon_U)}$ (@sec-demand). The
shadow price is not exempted by `AlwaysExemptResLPGKer`, as legacy.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** section 1 row `shpx` (Formulas E113), subsector rows `shp` (E457; legacy row 2377).
- **CPAT Python:** `policies.py` (`shpx`), `fuel_use.py`, `prepare()` (`shp`).
:::

## Pigouvian components {#sec-pr-pigou}

The model can compute an efficient (Pigouvian) tax per price unit: the cost of the local air pollution, the climate
damage and the road-transport externalities of one more unit of the fuel. Here they are prices; their welfare use and
the efficient prices of the subsidy estimates are in @sec-fiscal. The methodology describes the external costs in
[section 3.7.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#energy-externalities-costs).

The components are computed in every run; they enter prices only if ScenarioDefinition `AddEfficientTaxes` = Yes,
which CPAT Python does not support yet (@sec-pr-leftout). All are by price code $c$ (the 12 blocks and the two
electricity rows) in USD per price unit ([A1.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A1-2)).

### Phase-in {#sec-pr-pigphase}

$$
\phi_t = \min\!\left(\frac{\max(t - T_0 + 1,\ 0)}{\max(n,\ 1)},\ 1\right)
$$ {#eq-pr-pigphi}

where $\phi_t$ is the phase-in share (code `pig.phi`), $T_0$ the carbon-pricing start year (`CPIntro`) and $n$
`AddEfficientTaxesPhaseInYears`.

### Air pollution {#sec-pr-pigap}

The marginal damage of air pollution per GJ of fuel $f$ in subsector $s$ is the value of averted PM2.5 times the PM2.5
concentration one GJ adds:

$$
mc^{ap}_{s,f,t} = v_t\;\Big[(1 - w_t)\,d^{(0)}_{s,f} + w_t\,d^{(1)}_{s,f}\Big]\;\frac{10^9}{\theta \cdot 10^6}
$$ {#eq-pr-apmc}

where

- $mc^{ap}_{s,f,t}$ is the marginal air-pollution damage (code `airpol.mc`, USD/GJ; power: by plant type);
- $v_t$ is the value of averted modelled ambient PM2.5 (code `pig.vpm`, USD billion per µg/m³, from the air pollution
  module, typed FromAirPollution; the base year reads the next year, because legacy has no change in PM2.5 in 2022);
- $d^{(0)}$, $d^{(1)}$ are the µg/m³ per ktoe of the fuel: the module's concentration coefficients $\kappa$ of the
  source (road, ground level for residential, services and construction, food, other; coal, gas and other power
  plants) times the combustion emission factors of each pollutant, with base-year and final (`EFEndYear`, 2039)
  factors;
- $w_t$ is the weight of the final factors (code `pig.efw`): `EFFinShare` × $(t - t_0)/(\text{EFEndYear} - t_0)$,
  with `EFFinShare` 0 for constant factors, 1 for variable and 0.5 otherwise;
- $\theta$ is PJ per ktoe.

By price code (code `pig.ap`), the subsector damages are averaged with base-year fuel use as weights (the plain
average where all weights are 0) and converted to price units:

| Price code | Average over | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `coa.pow`, `nga.pow` | the power plant type | per GJ |
| `coa.res` | residential, food, services | only if base-year coal use of buildings exceeds `ApCoalResMin` (0.001) × all buildings fuel use |
| `nga.res` | residential, food, services | |
| `coa.ind`, `nga.ind` | the 8 industry subsectors | |
| `gso.all`, `die.all`, `lpg.all`, `ker.all` | the 16 oil-using subsectors (road, rail, aviation, navigation, residential, food, services, 8 industry, other energy use) | × GJ per liter |
| `oop.all` | other-oil power plants | × GJ per barrel (L194 fixed) |
| `ecy.res`, `ecy.ind`, `bio.all` | | 0 (issue I119) |

### Climate {#sec-pr-pigclimate}

$$
cc_{c,t} = SCC^{nat}_t\;\overline{ef}_{f(c)}\;u_c
$$ {#eq-pr-pigcc}

where $cc_{c,t}$ is the climate damage per price unit (code `cc.code`), $SCC^{nat}_t$ the national social cost of
carbon ([M1.6](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M1-6)) and $\overline{ef}_f$ the generic, uncalibrated CO2 factor of the fuel
(averaged over its emission-factor sectors; IEA for other oil products; issue I116).

### Road transport {#sec-pr-pigtr}

Accidents, congestion and road damage are costs per vehicle-km. The model turns them into costs per liter with the
base-year kilometres driven per liter of the fuel's total use, then lets them grow with the cost per km:

$$
tr_{c,t} = \sum_{k} cost^{km}_{k,t_0}\;kpl_f\;\big(1 - \omega_f\big)^{[k = rdm]}\;\frac{cost^{km}_{k,t}}{cost^{km}_{k,t_0}}, \qquad kpl_f = \overline{fe}_f\;\mu_f\;\rho_f
$$ {#eq-pr-pigtr}

where

- $tr_{c,t}$ is the road-transport cost per liter (code `pig.tr`; gasoline: accidents and congestion; diesel: also
  road damage, for the freight share only, issue I118; 0 for the other price codes);
- $cost^{km}_{k,t}$ is the cost per vehicle-km of kind $k$ (accidents, congestion, road damage) from the transport
  co-benefits module (typed FromTransportCB); the ratio is the growth against the base year (codes `pig.trg.*`);
  the products $cost^{km}_{k,t_0}\,kpl_f$ are the base-year costs per liter (codes `pig.trb.*`);
- $\overline{fe}_f$ is the base-year fuel economy (code `pig.fe0`, km/liter): passenger and light vehicles weighted by
  ownership, then mixed with 2-3 wheelers (gasoline) or freight (diesel) by the share $\omega_f$;
- $\omega_f$ is the passenger and light share of the road use of the fuel (code `pig.wsh`): gasoline 1 − the cycle
  share; diesel 1 − freight / (1 − bus);
- $\mu_f$ is the driving share of the fuel's response (code `pig.mu0`): gasoline
  $\varepsilon_U / (\varepsilon_U + \varepsilon_F)$; diesel
  $(\varepsilon^{die}_U + \omega(\varepsilon^{gso}_U - \varepsilon^{die}_U)) / (\varepsilon^{die}_U + \varepsilon^{die}_F + \omega(\varepsilon^{gso}_U + \varepsilon^{gso}_F - \varepsilon^{die}_U - \varepsilon^{die}_F))$;
- $\rho_f$ is the base-year road share of the fuel's use over all subsectors (code `pig.rsh0`).

### The Pigouvian tax and its netting {#sec-pr-pignet}

$$
pigx_{c,t} = \phi_t\left(ap_{c,t} + \mathbb{1}[\texttt{ClimateEffTax}]\;cc_{c,t} + tr_{c,t}\right)
$$ {#eq-pr-pigx}

where $ap_{c,t}$ is the air-pollution cost per price unit (`pig.ap`). With `AddEfficientTaxes` = Yes the gross new
excise $ntxg = fpr + pigx$ (@eq-pr-ntxb) is netted against the existing taxes, so the Pigouvian tax tops up what is
already there:

$$
F^x_{c,t} = \mathbb{1}[o \ne B]\;\min\!\Big(ntxg_{c,t},\ \max\big(0,\ ntxg_{c,t} - xpre_{c,t}\,u_c\big)\Big), \qquad
xpre_{c,t} = txo_{c,t} + pcsw_{c,t} + ppcw_{c,t} + xcpb_{c,t}
$$ {#eq-pr-pigntx}

where

- $xpre_{c,t}$ is the existing taxes before new policy of the block (code `xpre`, USD/GJ; 0 for electricity);
- $xcpb_{c,t} = \overline{ef}_f\,(XT\,\varphi^{ct}_t + XE\,\varphi^{ets}_t - XCP^0)$ is the change in existing carbon
  pricing of the block, at the generic emission factor and the block's own ECP sector and fuel (code `xcpb`; 0 for
  electricity).

The block's ECP key for `xcpb`: coal and gas by price sector; gasoline and diesel transport; LPG, kerosene and
biomass buildings; other oil products industry.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: Pigouvian components"}
```
for t in years:
    phi[t] = min(max(t - CPIntro + 1, 0) / max(PhaseInYears, 1), 1)
    w[t] = EFFinShare * (t - t0) / (EFEndYear - t0)
    vpm = air_vpm[max(t, t0 + 1)]
    for (s, f) in airpol_rows:
        mc[s, f, t] = vpm * ((1 - w[t]) * d0[s, f] + w[t] * d1[s, f]) * 1e9 / PJperKtoe / 1e6
for c in price_codes_14:
    for t in years:
        ap = weighted_average(mc[rows_of(c), t], weights=ener0) * u[c]     # table above
        cc = scc_nat[t] * ef_generic[fuel(c)] * u[c]
        tr = sum(trb[k, fuel(c)] * trg[k][t] for k in kinds(c))            # gso, die only
        pigx[c][t] = phi[t] * (ap + (cc if ClimateEffTax == 'Yes' else 0) + tr)
        xcpb[c][t] = ef_generic[fuel(c)] * (XT[c][col] * xct_p[t] + XE[c][col] * xets_p[t] - XCP0[c])
        xpre[c][t] = txo[c][t] + pcsw[c][t] + ppcw[c][t] + xcpb[c][t]
        ntxg[c][t] = fpr[c][t] + (pigx[c][t] if AddEfficientTaxes == 'Yes' else 0)
        if AddEfficientTaxes == 'Yes':
            ntxb[c][t] = min(ntxg[c][t], max(0, ntxg[c][t] - xpre[c][t] * u[c]))
        else:
            ntxb[c][t] = ntxg[c][t]
        ntxb[c][t] *= (scenario > 1)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}

  `pig.fe0`, `pig.wsh`, `pig.mu0`, `pig.rsh0`, `pig.kpl`, `pig.trg.*`, `pig.trb.*`, `pig.ap`, `cc.code`, `pig.tr`,
  `pigx`, `ntxg`, `xcpb`, `xpre`, `ntxb` (Formulas E34-E57). Inputs: ScenarioDefinition `AddEfficientTaxes` (MTInputs
  row 217), `ClimateEffTax` (216), `AddEfficientTaxesPhaseInYears` (212), `ExternalityAddVAT` (218, used by the
  efficient prices of @sec-fiscal).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/pigouvian.py`, `prepare()` (all rows but `ntxg`, `ntxb`); `policies.py`
  (`ntxg`, `ntxb`); equation A1.2. `AddEfficientTaxes` = Yes raises `NotImplementedError`.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **I104 (departs, user decision).** Legacy's air-pollution unit costs are average damages; the model uses marginal
  damages from the module's concentration coefficients.
- **I113 (replicated).** The Pigouvian tax tops up existing taxes, and the climate component can be charged on top of a
  carbon tax (climate charged twice), as legacy (legacy rows 8782, 8805, ... 9012).
- **I116 (replicated).** Climate damage per unit is the national SCC × a generic emission factor.
- **I118, I119 (replicated).** Road damage only for diesel; the electricity Pigouvian tax is always 0.
- **I151 (departs, user decision).** The road-transport component is the base-year value × the growth of the per-km
  costs, a proxy of scenario 1.
- **L194 (fixed).** Legacy adds an air-pollution cost in USD/GJ to the per-barrel price of other oil products.
- **L195, L196 (fixed).** Legacy has no phase-in in 2022-2024 and divides by 0 when the phase-in years are 0; one
  formula now holds in every year with $\max(n, 1)$.
:::

## Average prices and price indices {#sec-pr-averages}

Prices differ by subsector, so a single price per fuel needs weights. The model reports two kinds of averages: the
average new-policy wedges of each price block, and average prices and price indices by fuel. Both are computed in the
year loop, because they read fuel use. The methodology's aggregate price is the fuel-use weighted average
([section 3.2.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PricesAggregation)).

### New policies by price block {#sec-pr-blockavg}

Over the subsectors $s \in c$ priced by block $c$, weighted by their fuel use $F_{s,f}$ (ktoe):

$$
\bar{p}_c = \frac{\sum_{s \in c} p_{s,f}\,F_{s,f}}{\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f}}
$$ {#eq-pr-rpn}

where $\bar{p}_c$ is the retail price including new taxes and subsidies of the block (code `rpn`; $p^0_c$ where the
subsectors use none; [A2.6](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A2-6)). The block also shows:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pnq` | $\sum_{s \in c} F_{s,f}$, the weights (ktoe) |
| `pctx`, `etsnew`, `pntx`, `pxcd` | fuel-use weighted averages of `ctxnew`, `ets`, `ntx`, `xcpd` |
| `pnce` | $\bar{p}_c - p^0_c$, the total new policy including VAT |
| `pvatn` | `pnce` − (`pctx` + `etsnew` + `pntx` + `pxcd` + `pcsw` + `ppcw`): the VAT on the new policies and wedges, and the effect of the price floor |

These are weighted averages with each scenario's own quantities, not price indices.

### Average prices and indices by fuel {#sec-pr-indices}

For each fuel (coal, gas, gasoline, diesel, LPG, kerosene, jet fuel, other oil products, biomass), for electricity
and for all energy, the model sums over the 16 subsectors (electricity: the residential and industry user groups).
Subscript 1 is scenario 1 in the same year; subscript 0 is the base year, whose quantities and prices are data and so
equal in every scenario.

| Code | Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `pav.sp` | $\sum_s p\,F$ | spending, own quantities |
| `pav.q` | $\sum_s F$ | fuel use |
| `pav.uv` | $\sum p\,F / \sum F$ | average price (unit value) |
| `pav.spr` | $\sum_s p\,F_1$ | spending at scenario-1 quantities |
| `pav.las` | $\sum p\,F_1 / \sum p_1 F_1$ | **price index against scenario 1** (Laspeyres; scenario 1 = 1) |
| `pav.sp0` | $\sum_s p\,F_0$ | spending at base-year quantities |
| `pav.time` | $\sum p\,F_0 / \sum p_0 F_0$ | **price index over time** (base year = 1) |
| `pav.mix` | $(uv / uv_1) / las$ | mix effect: what the unit-value ratio adds to the price index |
| `pav.leg` | below | average price as legacy |
| `pav.lidx` | $leg / leg_1$ | legacy average price against scenario 1 (`pav.las` for fuels without a legacy average) |
| `pav.idx` | Settings `AveragePriceMethod` | **price index reported** (MTOutputs `mit.pav.idx`): *Legacy\** = `pav.lidx` (default), *Laspeyres* = `pav.las` |
| `rpe` | `pav.uv` of all energy | average retail energy price |

: Average prices and price indices by fuel {#tbl-pr-pav}

The unit-value ratio against scenario 1 equals the price index times the mix effect. Legacy reports the unit-value
ratio as the price change (issue I31); here the two parts are separate.

$$
\frac{uv}{uv_1} = las \times mix, \qquad las = \frac{\sum_s p_s\,F_{1,s}}{\sum_s p_{1,s}\,F_{1,s}}, \qquad time = \frac{\sum_s p_s\,F_{0,s}}{\sum_s p_{0,s}\,F_{0,s}}
$$ {#eq-pr-las}

**Units.** Fuels: USD/GJ × ktoe for spending, USD/GJ for the unit value. Electricity: USD/kWh and GWh. All energy:
spending in USD million (fuel spending × PJ per ktoe, plus electricity spending USD/kWh × GWh), fuel use in ktoe with
electricity converted (GWh × GJ per kWh / PJ per ktoe), so its unit value is in USD million per ktoe.

**The legacy average** (`pav.leg`, legacy rows 16293-16405):

- **Coal and gas** average three sector prices with **scenario-1 quantities of the same year**: residential `rpn`
  (weight: scenario-1 residential subsector use, `pavl.qr`), industry `rpn` (the 8 industry subsectors, `pavl.qi`),
  and power (weight: scenario-1 power generation fuel use, `pavl.qp`). The power price is the pre-policy price plus
  the policy cost per GJ of the power type:
  $pp = p^0_{pow} + G \cdot M \cdot pc / (FU \cdot \theta)$ (code `pavl.pp`; $G$ generation in MWy, $M$ million kWh per
  MWy, $pc$ the new policy cost per kWh `xac`, $FU$ the power fuel use). This is a Laspeyres index on three sectors; it
  falls back to the unit value where the weights are 0.
- **Oil products** take the single price `rpn` of their `.all` block.
- **Electricity** averages residential and industry with each scenario's own consumption (= `pav.uv`).
- **Biomass, jet fuel and all energy** have no legacy average: their unit value, and their reported index is the
  Laspeyres one.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: averages (year loop, year t)"}
```
for c in PRICES:
    rows = [(s, f) for (s, f) in fuel_rows if price_block(s, f) == c]
    pnq[c] = sum(ener[s, f] for (s, f) in rows)
    wavg = lambda v: sum(v[s, f] * ener[s, f] for (s, f) in rows) / pnq[c] if pnq[c] else 0
    pctx[c], etsnew[c], pntx[c], pxcd[c] = wavg(ctxnew), wavg(ets), wavg(ntx), wavg(xcpd)
    rpn[c] = wavg(atp) if pnq[c] else pbc[c]
    pnce[c] = rpn[c] - pbc[c]
    pvatn[c] = pnce[c] - (pctx[c] + etsnew[c] + pntx[c] + pxcd[c] + pcsw[c] + ppcw[c])
for f in PAV_FUELS:                               # coa, nga, gso, die, lpg, ker, jfu, oop, bio
    sp  = sum(atp[s, f] * ener[s, f] for s in subsectors)
    q   = sum(ener[s, f] for s in subsectors)
    spr = sum(atp[s, f] * ener_scen1[s, f] for s in subsectors)
    sp0 = sum(atp[s, f] * ener_base_year[s, f] for s in subsectors)
    uv = sp / q;  las = spr / sp_scen1[f];  time = sp0 / sp_base_year[f]
    mix = (uv / uv_scen1[f]) / las
    leg = legacy_average(f)                       # coal, gas: res, ind, power at scenario-1 quantities
    lidx = leg / leg_scen1[f]
    idx = lidx if AveragePriceMethod.startswith('Leg') else las
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation section 2, rows `pnq` ... `rpn` by block and `pav.*`, `pavl.*`, `rpe` (Formulas
  E256-E281). Scenario-1 quantities are a lookup through header row 10 (the column of scenario 1 for each year,
  `INDEX(...,0,row 10)`). Settings C54 `AveragePriceMethod`.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/prices.py`, `averages()` (block `prices.averages` of the year loop, after
  `totals.energy`); equation A2.6.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **I31 (accepted).** Legacy's average prices mix price and composition changes (legacy F5c). The model reports the
  unit value, a Laspeyres index, a time index and the mix effect separately, and reports the legacy average as the
  default index (user decision 2026-10-18).
- **L77 (fixed).** Legacy's index rows read the wrong fuels, and its gas test reads the policy total.
:::

## What is left out {#sec-pr-leftout}

| Left out | Where it stands |
|---|---|
| Pigouvian taxes in the price (`AddEfficientTaxes` = Yes) | built in Excel-AI; CPAT Python stops with `NotImplementedError` |
| Manual per-unit excise on fossil fuels (methodology: "Add additional excise") | not built; `AdditionalExcise` adds the manual excise to electricity only (@sec-power) |
| Ad-valorem baseline taxes | taxes are fixed in both legacy and the model; legacy's flag is unused |
| Methodology option to remove existing excise taxes from the policy year | not in the model |
| Methodology VAT options (same VAT rate in residential and transport; externalities in the VAT base for the price) | not in the price build-up; `ExternalityAddVAT` is used by the efficient prices only (@sec-fiscal) |
| Fixed and floating portions averaged over five historical years (methodology) | the model, as legacy, projects from the single year $L$ |
| Total carbon price memo of the methodology (direct and indirect elements) | the model reports an implicit carbon price by fuel (`tcp`) with the revenues (@sec-fiscal) |
| Electricity prices, the electricity subsidy gap, its producer subsidy allocation and consumer subsidy options | power module (@sec-power) |
| Price of road CNG and the engineer road model's fuel prices | road transport (@sec-transport) |
